Vignette:
# Kofi's Story

Kofi was thirty-three when he arrived at the clinic, but the exhaustion in his eyes made him look older. He had been a tailor in Lagos before the attack—a man who took pride in precision, in the way fabric could be cut and stitched into something whole. That life felt now as though it belonged to someone else entirely.

The bombing had occurred two years earlier at a busy shopping complex in the Lekki district. Kofi had been there on a Tuesday afternoon, meeting a client to take measurements for a wedding suit. He remembered walking through the entrance, the air-conditioning, the hum of commerce. Then came the sound—not loud at first, but deep, a feeling before it was a noise. The floor tilted. Glass fell like rain. He remembered being on the ground, the taste of concrete dust, the weight of something across his legs. Then nothing. A blank space where minutes should have been. When memory resumed, there were sirens, and he was being carried by strangers, and his left leg was bleeding in a way that seemed very far away.

The physical injuries had healed within months. The fracture in his tibia, the lacerations across his back and shoulders—these resolved. But something else had not. Kofi had moved to America a year after the attack, hoping that distance and a fresh start would restore him to himself. Instead, the world had become a place of constant threat that he could not quite name or locate.

Now, as a tailor working out of a small shop in a strip mall in Atlanta, Kofi found himself unable to settle into the rhythms of his work. When customers entered, he positioned himself so that his back was against the wall behind his cutting table, his eyes able to track the door, the windows, the space between the racks of fabric and the register. If a client asked him to step away from that position—to move to the front of the shop, or to turn and face away while adjusting a garment—a cold dread would rise in his chest. He had come to believe that safety required constant visual control of his surroundings, and to surrender that control, even momentarily, was to invite catastrophe.

The scanning had become automatic. Kofi entered any enclosed space—his apartment, the shop, a restaurant—and his eyes moved first to the exits. Where could he go if something happened? Which path was clearest? This vigilance exhausted him, but the alternative—not knowing—felt impossible.

The memories themselves were fragmented and strange. Sometimes Kofi could recall the sequence of events with an almost clinical clarity: the entrance, the sound, the fall. But when he recounted these moments, he felt nothing. The narrative seemed to belong to a film he was watching, not to his own body, his own terror. Other parts of the event were simply gone. He could not remember how long he lay on the ground, or whether he had called out, or what the faces of the people around him looked like. The absence of these details tormented him—as if the gaps themselves were evidence of something wrong with him, some failure of mind or character.

At night, when he tried to sleep, the memories came as a loop: the entrance, the sound, the falling. Over and over, as if his mind were trying to force the missing pieces into place through repetition. He had begun spending three, four, sometimes five hours each night on his phone—scrolling through games, through videos, through anything that required just enough attention to keep his mind from settling into that groove. During the day, if the silence of his shop became too heavy, he would manufacture small conflicts with customers over measurements or pricing, anything to create a disturbance that broke the weight of his own thoughts.

He had stopped making plans. His sister in New Jersey had invited him to her daughter's graduation in the spring; he had not responded. A woman he had met at his mosque had suggested they get coffee; he had made an excuse and not followed up. To imagine a future felt like an act of arrogance, a presumption that he deserved continuity. He was certain now that he could not be trusted to protect himself or anyone else. The attack had revealed him as weak, as someone who could be broken by forces beyond his control. How could such a person build a life?

It was his sister who finally insisted. She had called him one evening and, without preamble, told him he needed to see someone. He had argued, but her voice carried a finality that he recognized. Last week, he had made the appointment. Now, sitting in the waiting room, Kofi positioned himself in a chair with a clear view of the door, and waited to begin the work of becoming whole again.
